newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - April 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - April 22.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- ALLIANCE & LEICESTER SHARES BEAT PREDICTIONS

Shares in Alliance & Leicester opened yesterday at 556p each, well above the forecast 520p and giving the 2.2 million A&L customers a windfall worth 1,415 pounds each. The price increase is attributed to retail buyers and not institutions, however, and prices could fall within days. Halifax, Woolwich and Northern Rock are the next societies due to float.
-- CO-OP SEEKS TO STRENGTHEN HAND AGAINST LANCA BID

Lennox Fyfe, chairman of the Co-operative Wholesale Society, is seeking support at the company's May annual meeting in his attempt to halt Lanica Trust from preparing a hostile bid against it. Fyfe said that if the board was unanimous, CWS would not be put up for sale. LT's owner Andrew Regan had previous takeover plans halted by a High Court injunction.
-- UK SPENDING ON BSE PROMPTS TWO AUDITS

The National Audit office and the European Court of Auditors are preparing separate investigations into the government's spending during the BSE crisis. The UK Labour party had claimed that large abattoirs made excessive money from payments made on the killing of all cattle over 30 months of age. The report is due by the end of the year and should calculate the means of obtaining future refunds from the EU.
-- COMPETITORS CHALLENGE DEUTSCHE TELEKOM

German telecoms companies Mannesmann Arcor and o.tel.o have made complaints against Deutsche Telekom, claiming the telecoms giant is unfairly exploiting its business. The chairman of o.tel.o believes DT is taking intentional measures to prevent his company offering better service at a lower price. Mannesmann Arcor has threatened to take the case before the European Commission if necessary.
-- BUSINESS COUNTS COST OF LATEST BOMB THREATS

Transport in many parts of London on Monday morning became impossible as bomb threats once again brought the city to a halt. Business and industry are currently attempting to calculate the costs in lost working hours and revenues because of the threats, and business organisations fear a terrorist campaign may threaten inward investment and hurt the capital's reputation as a financial centre. The London Chamber of Commerce and Industry say the costs and disruptions were "considerable".
-- CAR OUTPUT PRODUCTION FALLS 4.6 PERCENT

The Central Statistical Office has said UK car production from March 1996 compared with March 1997 fell 4.6 percent even though output remained 3.1 percent higher than last year. The head of Motor Manufacturers and Traders blamed the fall on the levelling of new car sales in the past two months, but said foreign demand for cars manufactured in the UK remains strong.
-- CORDIANT BACKS THREE-WAY SPLIT

Advertising group Cordiant has confirmed it will split three ways and is currently looking for a partner in its media buying business, Zenith Media Worldwide. The split is said to be best for business and will closely align the interests of shareholders and management. Cordiant chief executive Bob Seelert has said Zenith ownership may be diluted "for a network...that is twice as big and three times as profitable".
-- DRUG TRIAL SETBACK IS BLOW TO US BIOTECH INDUSTRY

What many had called the most important trial for the US biotech industry in 1997 has ended in failure as Myloral, Boston Auto-Immune's MS treatment, failed to pass crucial phase III testing, proving it to be no more than a placebo. The failure is the latest in a series of setbacks to hit the US biotech sector, following poor results from companies such as Scios, Alkermes and Oravax. The medical failures have led to stock market failures in the U.S., but Europe remains disaffected.
-- NATIONAL GRID 'DISAPPOINTED'

UK electricity transmission company National Grid has said it is disappointed it did not win the contract to manage the transmission grid in Kazakhstan. Swis-Swedish engineering group ABB Power Grid Consortium was awarded the 25-year contract despite announcements earlier in the year by National Grid that it had been named the preferred bidder.
-- PEARSON APPROACHED OVER AFR

Several Australian groups have approached media and information group Pearson to see if it was interested in obtaining stakes in the Australian Financial Review if it makes it to the market. Fairfax Group, owner of the Financial Review have shown no evidence that it wants to sell the weekly paper, but Pearson has made clear that it would be interested in a Financial Review stake should it become available.
